Cnidus
NYE-dus
proper noun / place
From the Greek Knidos, a headland and city of Caria in southwest Asia Minor, at the corner where ships turn toward Crete.

📖 Biblical Definition

Cnidus is the Carian headland against which Paul’s ship sailed slowly many days, scarce come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering them, so that they sailed under Crete over against Salmone. The place appears only once in Scripture, yet it is a true point on the map of providence. Cnidus controlled a strategic turn of Mediterranean navigation: vessels working west from Myra of Lycia had to round that point before the open run toward Crete and beyond. Luke’s seamanship is precise. The contrary wind that stalled them off Cnidus was no accident of plot; it was the means by which the voyage was pressed toward Fair Havens, the counsel of Paul, the refusal of the centurion, and at last the shipwreck that still landed the gospel on Malta and, finally, in Rome. Cnidus therefore teaches that delays under the lee of a pagan cape are not outside the decree of God. The church that only counts landings and not headwinds will misread the hand of the Lord. Sometimes progress is measured by the cape you cannot yet clear. The cape that would not yield to their sails still yielded to the larger purpose of God, who had appointed both the storm and the safe arrival of His witness.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Carian headland of Asia Minor; Paul’s ship, hindered by contrary winds, was forced past Cnidus toward Crete.

expand to see more

CNIDUS, a headland and city of Caria in SW Asia Minor.

It marked a critical turn for ships bound west from Lycia.

Paul’s vessel scarce came over against Cnidus for lack of wind.

From there they sailed under Crete over against Salmone.

The delay off Cnidus belongs to the chain of providence toward Rome.

📖 Key Scripture

Act 27:7 — "And when we had sailed slowly many days, and scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us, we sailed under Crete, over against Salmone;"

Act 27:8 — "And, hardly passing it, came unto a place which is called The fair havens ; nigh whereunto was the city of Lasea."

Act 27:9 — "Now when much time was spent, and when sailing was now dangerous, because the fast was now already past, Paul admonished them,"

Act 27:10 — "And said unto them, Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage, not only of the lading and ship, but also of our lives."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Cnidus is easy to skip as nautical color; Scripture sets it inside the wise delays of God on the road to Rome.

expand to see more

The corruption is the demand that every providence feel like acceleration. Cnidus rebukes that. The wind not suffering them is as much the Lord’s instrument as the open door at Philippi. Unbelief reads weather as chaos; faith reads it as governance. When modern readers treat Acts 27 as adventure fiction, they lose the doctrine of the passage: God keeps His promise through storms, bad counsel, and slow miles under a Carian cape.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What must be recovered is the conviction that biblical geography is not scenery for myth, but the real theatre of the LORD’s providence, judgment, and grace. The places of Scripture stand as witnesses that God acts in history, among real peoples, on real soil, for the glory of His name.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Cnidus is the Carian point where contrary winds turned Paul’s voyage under Crete toward the appointed shipwreck and Rome.

expand to see more

Greek — Knidos, Carian headland and city.

Navigation — turn point from Lycia toward Crete.

Acts 27 — scarce come over against Cnidus.

Wind — the wind not suffering them forced a new course.

Decree — delay serving the larger promise of witness.

Usage

"Paul’s ship scarce came over against Cnidus because of contrary winds."

"From Cnidus they sailed under Crete toward Salmone and Fair Havens."

"Cnidus shows that God rules even the slow miles of a voyage."
